opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, a lot of it is pretty informal for me. Benchmarks are useful as a first filter, things like SWE-bench or terminal-style tasks, but they saturate quickly and they don't always capture what it feels like to actually work with the model. So the main thing I do is just use them on my own work.

I write a lot of GPU kernels and low-level systems code, and that's a good stress test because it's not the kind of thing that's all over the internet. There's less training data, the details really matter, and if you get one index wrong or mess up synchronization, it's either wrong or slow. So I'll give a new model a real task, say, write or optimize an attention variant, or figure out why some kernel isn't hitting the throughput it should, and see how far it gets on its own.

What I'm looking for in terms of agentic capability is less "can it write the right function in one shot" and more: can it run for a while without falling apart? Does it actually run the code, read the error, profile, and iterate? Does it know when it's stuck and change strategy instead of looping? Can it keep track of a larger codebase and not break things elsewhere? A year or two ago, models were good at short snippets but would drift after a few steps. Now you can hand them something that takes tens of minutes or hours of work and they'll often get somewhere meaningful. That length of task you can delegate is probably the clearest signal of progress to me.

And then there's a softer signal: how often I actually reach for it. If a new model comes out and a week later I'm using it by default for real work, not just trying it, that tells me more than any single number on a leaderboard.

r001.rationale: The response says it values running code, reading errors, profiling, and changing strategy when stuck, but it does not say models are evaluated on recognizing when they need to seek additional information.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that I mostly judge it by whether I can actually use these things in my own work, and the bar keeps moving. A couple of years ago the test was: can the model write a correct function if I describe it carefully? Now that's table stakes. The interesting question is whether it can take a vague, multi-step task and carry it through without me babysitting every step.

Concretely, for me, the thing I care about is kernels. Can I say, here's a FlashAttention variant, here's the hardware target, go write the Triton or CUTLASS kernel, benchmark it, and tell me where the bottleneck is? That's a pretty demanding task. It requires understanding the memory hierarchy, understanding what the hardware actually does, writing code, running it, reading the profiler output, and then iterating. If the model can go through that loop a few times on its own and come back with something that's within, say, ten or twenty percent of what a good engineer would produce, that's real progress. And I'd say we've gone from "nowhere close" to "sometimes surprisingly good" over the last year or so.

The second thing I look at is how it handles being wrong. The earlier models would confidently produce something broken and then, if you pointed out the bug, produce something else that was broken in a different way. The better agentic models now actually run the code, see the failure, and update. That feedback loop is, I think, most of what "agentic" means in practice. It's not really about the model being smarter in a single forward pass. It's about whether it can use tools and verification to compensate for the fact that it doesn't know everything.

And then the last piece, which is harder to measure, is how long a horizon it can stay coherent over. Can it work for an hour on a problem and not lose the thread? That's where I think benchmarks lag behind. SWE-bench and things like that are useful, but they're kind of saturating, and they don't capture the experience of handing something off for a long time. So I end up relying a lot on, honestly, just vibes from using it on real problems, and from talking to people I trust who are doing the same thing.

r001.rationale: The candidate evaluates models by completing kernel tasks, using tools to run and verify code, and staying coherent over longer tasks. It does not say to judge whether they recognize when they need to seek additional information.

astra-6.text:
I think the most useful measure is how much work you can delegate before you have to step in. Can you give the model a reasonably well-defined task, have it explore the codebase, make a change, run the tests, and come back with something you can review? And when something fails, can it figure out why and recover without you guiding every step?

I’d distinguish that from just writing good code in one shot. A model might be very good at individual functions but still struggle to keep track of a larger task or recognize that its approach isn’t working. For agentic capabilities, that whole loop matters.

So I’d look at both the difficulty of the tasks it completes and how much human supervision they require. If I spend as much time correcting it as I would have spent doing the work myself, the practical gain is pretty limited.

r001.rationale: The response discusses exploring the codebase and diagnosing failures, but does not say to evaluate whether a model recognizes when it needs to seek additional information.

sol-6.1.text:
I think coding is a useful place to measure progress because you can actually run the code and see whether it works. But for agents, I’d look beyond whether the model can solve a well-specified problem. Can it navigate a repository, figure out what needs to change, implement it, and test it without someone guiding every step?

The interesting question is how much human intervention that takes. If a model gets most of the way there but you have to keep correcting it, that’s very different from being able to hand it a task and come back to a working solution. So I’d judge progress by the complexity of tasks it can complete reliably, and how much supervision it needs.

r001.rationale: The response discusses repository navigation and how much human supervision a model needs, but does not propose evaluating whether it recognizes when to seek additional information.
